newsitem.title: JAPAN: Recovery continues but tax rise having effect -- BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Recovery continues but tax rise having effect -- BOJ.

text.p: Japan's economy is continuing its recovery, although some effects of a tax increase on April 1 are beginning to be detected, Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Monday.

Matsushita said repercussions from "rush in" demand ahead of the rise in the sales tax were beginning to be seen, but said: "Basically, a gradual recovery trend is continuing on the back of firmness in capital spending."
Matsushita, speaking at the opening of a two-day meeting of BOJ branch managers, said although public expenditures continued to decrease, net exports remained on a rising trend.
Capital spending was maintaining solid growth.

He said private consumption was gradually recovering, but in some areas of consumption a decrease was beginning to be detected. This decrease was in reaction to higher demand seen ahead of the tax rise on April 1, he said.
Matsushita also said that production was continuing to rise and that the declining trend in prices was clearly coming to a halt.

He said a temporary slowdown of the economy was inevitable due to the effects of fiscal tightening measures. The government introduced fiscal tightening, including a rise in the sales tax and an ending of special income tax cuts, at the start of the new fiscal year on April 1.
But Matsushita said that, taking into account positive signs in production, incomes and spending, it was highly likely that the economic recovery would continue after this setback.
Taking into account such conditions in the economy, it was appropriate for the BOJ to maintain its present monetary policy, Matsushita said.
"We will continue to carry out monetary policy putting emphasis on strengthening the basis for the economic recovery," he said.

He said restructuring measures announced by Nippon Credit Bank Ltd and a planned merger of Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd and regional Hokkaido Bank Ltd, all announced on April 1, would contribute greatly to removing uncertainty over Japan's financial system.

He said he hoped for early enactment of legislation to reform the law governing the Bank of Japan. The revision, due to be discussed in the current session of parliament ending in June, would give the central bank more independence and make its policies and decision-making more transparent.
